title: Spectral Prioritized Sweeping in Non-stationary Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: Spectral Prioritized Sweeping in Non-stationary Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract Prioritized Sweeping (PS) accelerates model-based reinforcement learning by selecting backups according to Bellman residual magnitude. In nonstationary reward settings, however, the canonical priority score is shortsighted: after a localized reward shift, residuals propagate only through realized backups, so bottlenecked or topologically distant state estimates may remain static under a limited replanning budget. We introduce the Graph Topology Augmentation framework, which employ the graph’s resolvent and its diffusion semantic, to augment the inquired signal. Our application, Graph Topology Augmentation for Prioritized Sweeping (GTA-PS), or which the alias Spectral Prioritized Sweeping (SPS) might be more universal, provides a drop-in ordering score for the setting of fixed dynamics and changing state rewards. GTA-PS uses a smootherized policy, inducing a transition chain, with its in- and out-Laplacian. The standard priority key is augmented with a mixing of regularized Laplacian inverses diffusing the residual magnitude. Furthermore, the topology contribution is annealed by a scheduler based on the Second Largest Eigenvalue Modulus (SLEM), allowing its scale to adapt to the chain’s mixing regime. We prove that the forward potential coincides with geometric discounted residual propagation and show that GTA-PS gives active priority instantly to all states. Tabular experiments on FourRooms and GARNET domains demonstrate improved replanning efficiency over standard PS under both exact DP and Dyna-style host planners.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) improves general behavior by using a known or learned transition model for planning [ 59 , Ch. 8] . The agent benefits most when planning effort can be directed to the states that matter most, especially within a brittle planning budget. [ 61 , 30 ] . Prioritized Sweeping (PS, or Standard-PS as to distinguish from our introduced variants) addresses this by maintaining a queue of states keyed by Bellman or Temporal-Difference residual magnitude [ 42 , 45 ] . For each planning step, the state with the largest priority has its value estimate updated. After that, predecessors’ value estimates often increase in magnitude; their refreshed priorities have higher chance to be queried next. This effect encourages information propagation backward through the predecessor support graph. Although conceptually simple, the resulting sweep can improve update efficiency by several orders of magnitude compared to uniform random backups [ 68 ] . We focus our study in the case of nonstationary Markov Decision Process (MDP), where the transition dynamics are fixed but the state reward changes over time [ 44 ] . This setting appears whenever the navigation structure is comparatively stable but the task objective changes, as in goal-conditioned robotics [ 46 ] , dynamic pricing and operations settings [ 5 ] , and sequential recommendation problems [ 70 ] . The standard approach using residual priority is shortsighted and reactive , as most state order remain stale until the Bellman wave has propagated to them through concrete realized backups. Under the budget of K K updates between reward shifts, some topologically distant states may never be reached, regardless of how sophisticated the host planner is [ 59 ] . In the nonstationary setting of our focus, this creates a further hindsight effect: by the time the residual signal reaches distant regions, the reward information that triggered it may already be stale. The resulting value errors can then feed back into the planning–action loop, causing the host to allocate future updates according to outdated priorities, compound into a circular degradation of both planning quality and subsequent data collection [ 15 , 33 ] . Figure 1: A localized reward shift creates sparse residual at s r s_{r} . Standard PS is shortsighted: priority of distant states receives no information hints. GTA-PS adds a topology potential on the policy-induced graph, assigning priority to upstream states before predecessor pushes reach them. We propose to address the former hindrance – credit propagation – by utilizing the model as assignment guidance. The Graph Topology Augmentation (GTA) framework capture preferences of the agent’s navigation field using spectral operators. From that, we derive rich representations and signal preconditioning that can be used to augment available score-based decisions, such as credit assignment, or bandit identification. Graph Topology Augmentation for Prioritized Sweeping (GTA-PS) is an implementation of the GTA ideology for our nonstationary setting study, that augment the residual-keyed priority with an additive mixed terms constructed from directed Laplacian inverses. The method is broadly applicable to orthogonal techniques, such as functional approximation, partial observability, and model uncertainty.

sections.heading: Our contributions.
sections.text: • We formalize priority-based planning as a host-agnostic queue-management problem, making the priority definition a modular design choice. The revised planning module plugs seamlessly into both exact tabular (DP) and Dyna-style planners without modifying the host. • We introduce Graph Topology Augmentation (GTA), a general RL framework that applies spectral operators on policy-induced chains to produce topology-aware planning signals. • We present GTA-PS (with the alias SPS), a concrete GTA instantiation for nonstationary rewards. It augments residual priority with a directed regularized-Laplacian potential and a fixed forward/backward weight aggregation together with a SLEM-driven β t \beta_{t} scheduler that adapts topology gain to the chain’s mixing regime. • We prove key properties of the topology signal, including its numerical stability, the geometric discount and implicit importance sampling effects, plus SLEM adaptive capabilities. • We present a succint experimental evaluation, variating chain statistics across environments and planner architectures, with surgical ablations isolating each cause’s effectiveness.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: In model-based planning, three lines of work have been established to provide richer planning guidance beyond raw residual magnitude, aiding prioritized sweeping decision. Successor-based signals spread value information over the state graph rather than waiting for purely local error cascades [ 22 , 58 ] . Learned abstractions compress the planning space, utilizing the generalization capabilities of supervised learning, as in VaST ’s abstract tabular model [ 20 ] . Graph-structural heuristics uses auxiliary graph representation, as in TVI/FTVI , which exploit the strongly connected components decomposition of the MDP [ 21 ] . Together these demonstrate that good planning requires more than raw residuals and that model knowledge is a powerful source of leadership. Spectral graph theory has a long history of applications in RL representation learning. Proto-value functions [ 39 , 38 ] use undirected Laplacian eigenvectors as smooth value-approximation bases [ 55 , 7 ] . The same eigenvectors underpin option discovery [ 36 ] and its deep analogues via the successor representation [ 37 ] and cover-time options [ 32 ] . Scalable computational methods include Krylov-subspace methods such as Arnoldi and GMRES [ 27 , 48 ] , Graph-drawing objectives with unique solutions [ 66 ] , and recent exact recovery methods [ 28 ] . Recent concurrent work on effective resistance has proposed it as an intrinsic reward guiding agents toward structurally accessible goals [ 14 ] . In these works, spectral operators mainly serve as offline representation or filtering bases rather than as a direct mechanism for shaping online backup selection. Our proposed Graph Topology Augmentation framework brings analytical Markov-chain tools into an RL planning module. It builds on the Laplacian-potential intuition from electrical networks [ 24 ] , treating the policy-induced chain as the Laplacian kernel [ 19 ] and its Green’s function as the potential operator [ 18 ] . Eigenvalues of the directed chain [ 35 ] is utilized as a scheduling signal. Additionally, several analytical tools such as biorthogonal decomposition [ 29 ] , additive reversibility decomposition [ 12 ] , and classical spectral graph bounds [ 17 ] are investigated to further enrich the framework.

sections.heading: Markov Decision Processes.
sections.text: We consider a finite discounted MDP ℳ = ( 𝒮 , 𝒜 , p , r t , γ ) , \mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},p,r_{t},\gamma), with | 𝒮 | < ∞ |\mathcal{S}|<\infty , | 𝒜 | < ∞ |\mathcal{A}|<\infty , fixed discount γ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \gamma\in(0,1) , and a fixed transition kernel p ⁡ ( s ′ ∣ s , a ) p(s^{\prime}\mid s,a) . The reward is a bounded, state-based vector r t : 𝒮 → ℝ r_{t}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R} that may change over time . Non-station is introduced in the modeling process as demand permutations captured by the reward signal, while the navigation skeleton is asserted to be static.

sections.heading: Priority-based planning.
sections.text: A planning sweep can only be realistically implemented on a serial computer as a sequence of individual backups. Such updates poses to be more effective when performed in-place, so that later backups in the same sweep can immediately use earlier updates [ 59 , Ch.4] . Hence, one can go even further, by applying an ordering on backups, so that the overlapping effect is most utilized. Such order can be maintained programmatically in a priority queue, ensuring the queried element always hold the largest weight. The particular landscape of priority-based planning is more sophisticated, and we dedicate to describe them thoroughly in [ B.3 The unified Prioritized Sweeping interface , D.5 Baselines and fair-comparison controls ].

sections.heading: Agent setting.
sections.text: The host planner can vary: exact asynchronous value iteration or a Dyna-style planning loop. In both cases the planner maintains a value estimate, requiring efficient backup ordering. Such individual backup is denoted as a planning step , planned before the host decides to take a committal action (denoted as a host step ). In our paper, the number of planning step is fixed to K K per host step for fair comparisons. Our setting deliberately limits the use of prior knowledge, so that the agent is designed under minimal assumptions. The information available at initialization is either an oracle tabular model in the DP setting, or an immature learned model in the learning setting. Details of component settings in each host algorithm is discussed in B.1 Algorithmic settings for MDP observability .

sections.heading: Residuals as inferred belief.
sections.text: Residual (in short for value estimation residual ) measures the discrepancy between the planner’s current estimate and new, implied one by latest evidence. Formally, ξ t ​ ( s ) := | 𝒯 t ​ V t ​ ( s ) − V t ​ ( s ) | , \xi_{t}(s):=\left|\mathcal{T}_{t}V_{t}(s)-V_{t}(s)\right|, where 𝒯 t ​ V t ​ ( s ) \mathcal{T}_{t}V_{t}(s) is the value estimate inferred from the current reward and transition information. Prioritized sweeping treats residual magnitude as a belief-correction score: states with larger discrepancies are backed up first. The important caution is that the inferred estimation should be both unbiased and robust to variance, which limits the residual utilizing only one-step samples.

sections.heading: Graph Topology Augmentation framework
sections.text: As canonical planning techniques uses mixing techniques or representational kernels to artificially transmit the reactive signal, our GTA framework instead takes a topological-driven approach – informing decision processes by preconditioning signal with topological operator. The framework facilitates four roles: • proactive priority signal for guiding the algorithm 4.2 ; • detector of high-impact states and bottlenecks E.2 Additional ablations ; • scheduler for modulating the topology gain 4.2 ; • diagnostic tool for understanding the planning geometry A.2 Supporting Lemmas .

sections.heading: 6.1 Recovery and planning efficiency
sections.text: The main empirical result is that GTA-PS improves both planning accuracy, reward collection and shift recovery under the same planning budget. In the Dyna setting of Fig. 2 , both GTA variants reduce value error faster than Standard-PS across all tested state sizes and budgets, with the gain most visible immediately after each shift when reactive propagation is still local. Cumulative performance also holds. Fig. 3 shows that the per-episode error gap accumulates into a persistent advantage (Fig. 8 ), matching the interpretation of Thm. 5.1 . These results support the practical claim of greater sample efficiency under limited replanning. Figure 3: Cumulative tracking ablation under repeated reward shifts in GARNET. GTA-PS β lowers the per-episode terminal error, reduces cumulative tracking error TE ⁡ ( N ) \mathrm{TE}(N) , and produces a steadily increasing cumulative advantage over Standard-PS. This is the theorem-facing empirical evidence for persistent advantage under frequent reward shifts.

sections.heading: 6.2 Robustness and Recommendations
sections.text: Ablations on fixed, varied α = α t \alpha=\alpha_{t} and β = β t \beta=\beta_{t} in Appendix D.8 Additional experiment results. show that moderate β \beta improves the agreement between the topology field and the realized pop order, while oversized β \beta sharply degrades. This is consistent with the convergence logic of Prop. 5.1 : the topology term is most useful as a bias that surfaces blocked states early and not as a replacement for residual-driven prioritization. Complementary α \alpha sweeps also favor small backward mixing. In practice we therefore tune GTA-PS with small α \alpha and moderate β \beta . Extended stochasticity, transport, and bottleneck audits are investigated to Appendix D.8 Additional experiment results. . The common lesson is environment adaptability: GTA-PS remains effective in stochastic GARNET instances and in bottlenecked FourRooms layouts, but a custom, highly adversarial transport can render topological guidance clueless. The best of both worlds is to keep topology guidance as an adaptive bias rather than a hard replacement for residual priority.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: Our GTA framework utilizes graph-theoretic foundations to craft representation operators that capture entities of interest. By leveraging these tools, GTA therefore can capture subtle patterns of connectivity, influence, and community structure that are not visible from simple degree counts or path-based metrics. On top of this spectral foundation, GTA-PS employs learned models to map beliefs in both the model and the policy into a rich structural priority score. Within the technique, we provide intensive theoretical analysis and surgical experiments to reveals its profound ground. We hope to further extend the framework to other settings, as well as combine it with orthogonal advances in representation learning, exploration, and scalable planning.

sections.heading: A.1 Analytical assumptions
sections.text: First we address some stronger behaviorial assumptions or workarounds applied to ensure robustness throughout our analytics. Assumption 1 (Communicating MDP) . The MDP ℳ = ( 𝒮 , 𝒜 , p , ℛ , γ ) \mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},p,\mathcal{R},\gamma) has finite state and action spaces and is communicating : for any two states s , s ′ ∈ 𝒮 s,s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S} , there exists a stationary policy under which s ′ s^{\prime} is reachable from s s with positive probability. Equivalently, every ε \varepsilon -soft stationary policy induces an irreducible transition matrix on 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . Since the Boltzmann policy design in 4.2 assigns nonzero probability to every action, the induced transition matrix P t P_{t} is irreducible for all t t . Assumption 2 (Bounded reward signal) . Rewards may be stochastic and may change exogenously over time, but their absolute value do not exceed Δ max \Delta_{\max} . This keeps residuals, value targets, and topology scores finite. sections.heading: B.1 Algorithmic settings for MDP observability
sections.text: As to aid the integration of GTA-PS onto DP and Dyna, we can not ignore what each of them is built for in the first place. DP can only be chosen when the full oracle distributional setting is exposed. The host agent’s belief cannot exceed that of exact planning model, as every intel: the known transition kernel, the current reward distribution, and the ideal Bellman residual can be traced at ease. The host does not need exploratory action selection onto the MDP to collect data. The one actual committal process – being Policy Improvement – serves as the host step. In the sample-based Dyna setting, because of 3 , the host agent’s belief must be empirical: it can only be formed through observed experience, by typically maintaining a learned model plus the current reward estimate. The available information is therefore local and noisy, best managed by one-step TD residuals rather than other more sample consuming ones. The host step is action execution under an exploratory move, as this leads for subsequent learning process. Note. In Dyna, the host policy should be an ε \varepsilon -greedy one, so that new experience continues to update the sample model and not get stuck in stale knowledge.

sections.text: The safest way to read the deployed module is as a directed acyclic computation graph. At a fixed host step, the topology-policy state determines the induced topology kernel and its two linear systems: π t PS ⟶ P t ⟶ ( L t o ​ u ​ t , L t i ​ n ) . \pi_{t}^{\mathrm{PS}}\;\longrightarrow\;P_{t}\;\longrightarrow\;(L_{t}^{out},L_{t}^{in}). sections.heading: B.3 The unified Prioritized Sweeping interface
sections.text: We should view any priority-based system as a database for the host. The host agent gains complete control over when entries are pushed, queried, refreshed, and removed during planning. The priority module should exposes a small set of stateful operations that the host can invoke inside DP or Dyna-style procedures, while preserving the same residual and topology bookkeeping across all variants. This makes the interface reusable across different replanning schedules, reward-update patterns, transition models and stopping rules. We do not specify how this should be implemented programmatically. However you can see the GTA-PS + DP/Dyna pseudocode in E.1 Dyna/DP + GTA-PS pseudocode for the concrete host-side call sequence.

sections.heading: B.4.1 Residual gating mechanism
sections.text: GTA-PS precautiously mix topology as an ordering correction specifically over the residual support. At each planning step, define the residual-active set ℐ t ≜ { s ∈ 𝒮 : | ξ t ​ ( s ) | > 0 } . \mathcal{I}_{t}\triangleq\{s\in\mathcal{S}:|\xi_{t}(s)|>0\}. If ℐ t ≠ ∅ \mathcal{I}_{t}\neq\varnothing , the next backup state is selected only from ℐ t \mathcal{I}_{t} : s t ∈ arg ⁡ max s ∈ ℐ t ​ { | ξ t ​ ( s ) | + β t ​ τ t ​ ( s ) } . s_{t}\in\arg\max_{s\in\mathcal{I}_{t}}\left\{|\xi_{t}(s)|+\beta_{t}\tau_{t}(s)\right\}. and if not, exploratory action is triggered to collect more data. Thus the topology term β t ​ τ t ​ ( s ) \beta_{t}\tau_{t}(s) can reorder states that already have positive Bellman residual, but it cannot select a topology-only state while residual-active states exist. This residual gate gives the anti-starvation arguments [ 10 , 64 ] , needed for the asynchronous contraction proof. Therefore GTA-PS preserves the standard infinite-residual visit condition used by asynchronous value-iteration convergence arguments.

sections.heading: B.5 Complexity analysis.
sections.text: The complexity story splits cleanly into a local per-backup cost and three optional amortized corrections: a standalone dense τ \tau refresh, a dense topology-operator rebuild, and an Arnoldi/SLEM sync. The local cost is paid on every host backup and comes from PopAndPrioritize , the Bellman or TD backup itself, PushPredecessors , and, in the online Sherman–Morrison regime, the row-local TopologyUpdate . The amortized terms are paid only when one of the dense refresh or spectral-sync events is triggered. For bookkeeping, write C τ = O ⁡ ( C pot + | 𝒮 | + q t + | ℐ t | ) C_{\tau}\;=\;O\!\bigl(C_{\mathrm{pot}}+|\mathcal{S}|+q_{t}+|\mathcal{I}_{t}|\bigr) for one RefreshTau call: the resolvent solves, dense mixing, top- q t q_{t} extraction, and queue rebuild/rekey. Let C arn = O ⁡ ( j ​ | 𝒮 | ⋅ deg + j 2 ​ | 𝒮 | ) C_{\mathrm{arn}}\;=\;O\!\bigl(j|\mathcal{S}|\cdot\mathrm{deg}+j^{2}|\mathcal{S}|\bigr) for one Arnoldi recomputation with Krylov depth j j , let C topo C_{\mathrm{topo}} denote the cost of one dense policy-dependent topology rebuild after batching row changes, and let C shift = O ⁡ ( C res + C τ ) C_{\mathrm{shift}}\;=\;O\!\bigl(C_{\mathrm{res}}+C_{\tau}\bigr) for one reward shift, since a shift recomputes the host residual field and then refreshes τ \tau but does not change P t P_{t} or require a fresh Arnoldi pass. If a particular implementation couples some of these events, the corresponding costs simply merge; the split here is only to keep the accounting explicit. The relevant granularity for the host planner is therefore one plan step or one backed-up state. For DP, the exact per-backup cost with GTA-PS is C DP ​ ( s ) = O ⁡ ( | 𝒜 | ⋅ deg + | Pred ⁡ ( s ) | ​ log ⁡ | 𝒮 | + log ⁡ | 𝒮 ​ | + log ⁡ q t + | ​ 𝒮 | ) , C_{\mathrm{DP}}(s)=O\!\Bigl(|\mathcal{A}|\cdot\mathrm{deg}+|\mathrm{Pred}(s)|\log|\mathcal{S}|+\log|\mathcal{S}|+\log q_{t}+|\mathcal{S}|\Bigr), where the O ⁡ ( | 𝒜 | ) O(|\mathcal{A}|) row-softmax term is absorbed. Relative to residual-only PS, the extra GTA-PS overhead per DP plan step is therefore tightly bounded by O ⁡ ( log ⁡ q t + | 𝒮 | ) O(\log q_{t}+|\mathcal{S}|) . For one Dyna simulated planning backup, the same expression holds with the Bellman-style term replaced by the TD-style host cost. The dense τ \tau refresh, dense topology rebuild, Arnoldi sync, and reward-update terms are secondary amortized corrections to this dominant local plan-step term. If standalone τ \tau refreshes are triggered every T τ T_{\tau} host backups, dense topology rebuilds every T topo T_{\mathrm{topo}} host backups, Arnoldi is rerun every T arn T_{\mathrm{arn}} host backups, and reward shifts arrive with characteristic scale T T , then the full per-step DP cost admits the upper bound C DP full ​ ( s ) = C DP ​ ( s ) + O ⁡ ( C τ T τ + C topo T topo + C arn T arn + C shift T ) . C_{\mathrm{DP}}^{\mathrm{full}}(s)\;=\;C_{\mathrm{DP}}(s)\;+\;O\!\Bigl(\frac{C_{\tau}}{T_{\tau}}\;+\;\frac{C_{\mathrm{topo}}}{T_{\mathrm{topo}}}\;+\;\frac{C_{\mathrm{arn}}}{T_{\mathrm{arn}}}\;+\;\frac{C_{\mathrm{shift}}}{T}\Bigr). For a Dyna host agent, one real environment interaction is followed by K K simulated planning backups. The base per-interaction cost, excluding periodic sync overhead, is C Dyna = O ⁡ ( | 𝒜 | + K ⋅ [ | Pred ⁡ ( s ) | ​ log ⁡ | 𝒮 | + log ⁡ | 𝒮 ​ | + log ⁡ q t + | ​ 𝒮 | ] ) , C_{\mathrm{Dyna}}\;=\;O\!\Bigl(|\mathcal{A}|\;+\;K\cdot\bigl[|\mathrm{Pred}(s)|\log|\mathcal{S}|+\log|\mathcal{S}|+\log q_{t}+|\mathcal{S}|\bigr]\Bigr), where the O ⁡ ( | 𝒜 | ) O(|\mathcal{A}|) term is the real-step TD update and model learning, and the K K factor scales the local plan-step overhead. To this base cost, each interaction adds its share of periodic work, proportional to the K + 1 K+1 host steps it contributes. Contributing the maintaining overhead makes the realized cost on each host step become: C Dyna full = C Dyna + O ⁡ ( ( K + 1 ) ​ [ C τ T τ + C topo T topo + C arn T arn ] + C shift T ) . C_{\mathrm{Dyna}}^{\mathrm{full}}\;=\;C_{\mathrm{Dyna}}\;+\;O\!\Bigl((K+1)\Bigl[\tfrac{C_{\tau}}{T_{\tau}}+\tfrac{C_{\mathrm{topo}}}{T_{\mathrm{topo}}}+\tfrac{C_{\mathrm{arn}}}{T_{\mathrm{arn}}}\Bigr]\;+\;\tfrac{C_{\mathrm{shift}}}{T}\Bigr). The first three terms scale with K K because both the real step and all K K simulated backups advance the host-step counters for τ \tau refresh, topology rebuild, and Arnoldi cadence. The reward-shift term is independent of K K since shifts arrive relatively to the host step. sections.heading: Why nonstationary reward is the chosen setting
sections.text: With stationary reward, standard PS runs to convergence. At convergence ξ t → 𝟎 \xi_{t}\to\mathbf{0} , so 𝐟 t o ​ u ​ t = ( L t o ​ u ​ t + η ​ I ) − 1 ​ ξ t → 𝟎 \mathbf{f}^{out}_{t}=(L^{out}_{t}+\eta I)^{-1}\xi_{t}\to\mathbf{0} and the topology signal vanishes identically (asymptotic-zero property). For deterministic shortest-path problems, Dijkstra’s algorithm computes the optimal policy in O ⁡ ( | 𝒮 | ​ log ⁡ | 𝒮 | + | E | ) O(|\mathcal{S}|\log|\mathcal{S}|+|E|) – strictly superior. Though GTA-PS can excel in both settings, the contribution are not enough to compensate both the computational cost and the enormous potential of the new queue system. Nonstationary reward with bottlenecks is the setting where GTA-PS dominates. When r t r_{t} shifts at frequency 1 / T 1/T , the planner has T T steps before the next shift. A full PS sweep costs O ⁡ ( | 𝒮 | 2 ​ | 𝒜 | ) O(|\mathcal{S}|^{2}|\mathcal{A}|) ; under budget T ≪ | 𝒮 | 2 ​ | 𝒜 | T\ll|\mathcal{S}|^{2}|\mathcal{A}| , the Bellman wavefront has not reached all states and the reactive residual signal is zero at predecessor-blocked states. GTA-PS’s topology signal is nonzero at all states immediately after a reward shift (Prop. 5.3 in the main text), so it can prioritize predecessor-blocked states before the wavefront arrives. The sub- O ⁡ ( | 𝒮 | 2 ) O(|\mathcal{S}|^{2}) multiplier ensures the economy, while the empirical efficiency outperform standard PS in numerous competing domains.

sections.heading: Why the resolvent, among the diffuser family?
sections.text: There are numerous choices for a diffuser operator, such as k k -truncated smoothing ( I − η ​ L ) k (I-\eta L)^{k} , heat diffusion exp ⁡ ( − τ ​ L ) \exp(-\tau L) , the Laplacian pseudoinverse, and the regularized resolvent. GTA-PS uses the resolvent because it is both controllable and economical. • Truncated smoothing has a hard finite horizon, heat diffusion is costly to update incrementally, and the pseudoinverse lacks explicit horizon control while depending on the Laplacian nullspace. In contrast, the resolvent ( L + η ​ I ) − 1 (L+\eta I)^{-1} has η \eta naturally acts as a geometric discounting factor. • Resolvent has a concise, exact localized update formula in B.2 Computational methods , which we believe would be nontrivial for heat diffusion or pseudoinverse to possess.

sections.heading: Why low-rank update assumption?
sections.text: A topology-policy change at state s upd s_{\mathrm{upd}} induces a row-local perturbation δ ​ P t = e s upd ​ w ⊤ \delta P_{t}=e_{s_{\mathrm{upd}}}w^{\top} . This is why low-rank resolvent identities are natural in the analysis: it adhere to learning process being local rather than global. However, this does not restrict the reward non-station capacity, as multiple localized shift can be batched in a vector shift facing host step.

sections.heading: Relative to competing topology-aware works.
sections.text: The same design choice also clarifies where GTA-PS differs from adjacent methods. Relative to standard PS and VaST [ 20 ] , GTA-PS is proactive: the resolvent field is dense immediately after a reward shift, so distant states can enter the queue before the Bellman wavefront reaches them. Relative to TVI/FTVI [ 21 ] , GTA-PS uses a soft, interruptible topology signal rather than an SCC batch schedule; it can be stopped after any backup and re-used after a reward shift without recomputing a decomposition. Relative to the successor representation [ 22 ] , reward updates remain cheap while the topology operator is applied through sparse linear solves rather than through storage of a full dense successor matrix.

sections.heading: Two-queue architecture with top- q q frontier.
sections.text: Because 𝝉 t = G ​ ξ t \boldsymbol{\tau}_{t}=G\xi_{t} is dense (nonzero everywhere when ξ t ≠ 𝟎 \xi_{t}\neq\mathbf{0} ), inserting it directly into the residual heap would crowd the queue with low-priority states, adding an excessive O ⁡ ( | 𝒮 | CLOSE O(|\mathcal{S}| cost multiplier. The simple solution is to limit the queue capacity by q q . Additionally, the implementation uses two heaps: 𝒬 ξ \mathcal{Q}_{\xi} over the active residual set and ℋ q \mathcal{H}_{q} over a filtered top- q q frontier extracted from the dense 𝒬 τ \mathcal{Q}_{\tau} . This decouples the two signals : the residual heap guarantees that states with large Bellman error remain eligible at all times, while the topology frontier injects proactive candidates without flooding the heap. Setting q t = | 𝒮 | q_{t}=|\mathcal{S}| recovers the unfiltered version analyzed theoretically.

sections.heading: Budget priority: residual-backups first.
sections.text: In PopAndPrioritize , residual-reducing backups are mandatory for convergence, while topology-only backups (states with ξ = 0 \xi=0 but τ > 0 \tau>0 ) are exploratory. Under tight budget, the implementation ensures that ℋ q \mathcal{H}_{q} never starves 𝒬 ξ \mathcal{Q}_{\xi} . This prevents the topology signal from consuming budget on no-op Bellman backups at already-converged states.

sections.heading: LU factorization threshold.
sections.text: For small state spaces, sparse LU factorization provides exact triangular solves at O ⁡ ( | 𝒮 | ) O(|\mathcal{S}|) each and is the default path in the tabular experiments. In the current code the threshold is explicit: _LU_THRESHOLD = 300 . Above that threshold the module switches to GMRES with a sparse-direct fallback. The exact crossover depends on sparsity structure, but the checked-in implementation address this cutoff cleanly.

sections.heading: Column cache abandoned.
sections.text: An earlier design maintained an explicit O ⁡ ( | 𝒮 | 2 ) O(|\mathcal{S}|^{2}) column cache 𝐠 s = G η , t o ​ u ​ t ​ ( ⋅ , s ) \mathbf{g}_{s}=G^{out}_{\eta,t}(\cdot,s) (the s s -column of the Green’s operator) to accelerate incremental updates. This was abandoned in favour of the Sherman–Morrison dual tri-solve approach: the column cache introduces O ⁡ ( | 𝒮 | 2 ) O(|\mathcal{S}|^{2}) memory and requires maintenance of O ⁡ ( | 𝒮 | ) O(|\mathcal{S}|) columns as the policy evolves, while the dual-solve approach achieves the same update expressiveness at O ⁡ ( | 𝒮 | ) O(|\mathcal{S}|) per step without any persistent column cache.

sections.heading: Stale-column incremental strategy.
sections.text: An intermediate design proposed maintaining stale approximate columns with periodic refresh, balancing O ⁡ ( | 𝒮 | ) O(|\mathcal{S}|) local cost against O ⁡ ( | 𝒮 | 2 ) O(|\mathcal{S}|^{2}) full recomputation. This was deemed unnecessary: the Sherman–Morrison formula provides exact updates at the same O ⁡ ( | 𝒮 | ) O(|\mathcal{S}|) cost without accumulation of refresh lag.

sections.heading: Full recomputation of in-field per policy step.
sections.text: The in-field perturbation δ ​ L t i ​ n = diag ⁡ ( w ) − w ​ e s upd ⊤ \delta L^{in}_{t}=\mathrm{diag}(w)-w\,e_{s_{\mathrm{upd}}}^{\top} is not rank-1, so Sherman–Morrison does not apply. An early implementation attempted to track 𝐟 i ​ n \mathbf{f}^{in} incrementally through a generalised rank- ( d + 1 ) (d+1) update; the fill-in in the update formula made this costlier than periodic batch recomputation. The settled design rebuilds 𝐟 i ​ n \mathbf{f}^{in} in batch at Arnoldi sync points, accepting O ⁡ ( | 𝒮 | ) O(|\mathcal{S}|) periodic cost amortised over T arn T_{\mathrm{arn}} steps.

sections.heading: Forced Arnoldi on every reward shift.
sections.text: An early version triggered a full SLEM recomputation (Arnoldi) at every reward shift. This was wasteful: the transition matrix P t P_{t} does not change at a reward shift (only 𝐫 t \mathbf{r}_{t} changes), so SLEM ⁡ ( P t ) \mathrm{SLEM}(P_{t}) and its eigendecomposition remain valid. The current design lets Arnoldi fire on its natural cadence T arn T_{\mathrm{arn}} , independent of reward shifts.

sections.heading: Forward-only ablation is not uniformly best.
sections.text: The repository keeps a dedicated forward-only comparison by setting α = 0 \alpha=0 inside the asymmetry sweeps (RQ4 and RQ6). Those scripts treat it as an ablation, not as the deployed default. This reflects the underlying design lesson: in directed environments, relying only on 𝐟 t out \mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{out}}_{t} can miss upstream source–sink structure that becomes visible once the backward field 𝐟 t in \mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{in}}_{t} is mixed in. The code therefore tunes a fixed α \alpha for the full GTA variants rather than collapsing the method to the forward-only special case.

sections.heading: LU fill-in at large | 𝒮 | |\mathcal{S}| .
sections.text: For very large state spaces, sparse LU factorization fill-in grows beyond memory or incurs prohibitive one-time cost. The GMRES fallback is present precisely for this regime. The checked-in benchmark scripts probe this overhead on FourRooms and on GARNET instances up to | 𝒮 | = 200 |\mathcal{S}|=200 ; future work should push that scaling study further and characterize the LU-to-iterative crossover as a function of transition sparsity rather than only of | 𝒮 | |\mathcal{S}| .

sections.heading: C.3 Limitations
sections.text: The current study is still limited to small-to-medium tabular domains. Although GTA-PS’s mechanism is sound and grounded, its scaling frontier on much larger state spaces is not addressed. Our experiments also focus on localized positive reward shifts. Empirically, the method is not uniformly strong under every perturbation: highly adversarial, drift-heavy, or spark-like transports can distort the topology signal and weaken guidance quality. On the algorithmic side, we validate mainly DP and Dyna-style hosts, leaving broader orthogonal integrations such as Dyna-2 or uncertainty-aware planners. Finally, GTA-PS incurs real wall-clock overhead from topology refreshes and queue maintenance, so the present paper demonstrates superior replanning under fixed backup budgets rather than lower raw compute cost.

sections.heading: Fast-shift asymptotics.
sections.text: In the regime ρ = T / t mix ​ ( 1 / 4 ) ≪ 1 \rho=T/t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\ll 1 (reward shifts arrive much faster than the chain can mix), it is conjectured that the mean per-episode advantage A ¯ \bar{A} grows as 1 / ρ 1/\rho . A formal scaling argument for this conjecture, together with empirical validation across the full K / t mix K/t_{\mathrm{mix}} ratio range in GARNET, would establish the precise operating regime where GTA-PS’s benefit is maximised relative to its computational cost.

sections.heading: Integration with learned models.
sections.text: The current theoretical analysis (Sections 5, 7) is confined to the exact-model setting (known p p ). Extending operator-norm bounds, decision-accuracy guarantees, and the ergodic cumulative advantage theorem to the learned-model case ( p ^ t \hat{p}_{t} with estimation error) would cover Dyna-style deployment, where model noise interacts with topology diffusion. The multi-step TD residual oracle (Appendix B.2) provides a practical interface; the formal gap remains.

sections.heading: SLEM as a continuous signal for other RL components.
sections.text: The SLEM serves here as a scheduling statistic for β t \beta_{t} . More broadly, SLEM and the resolvent-based topology potentials could inform exploration bonuses (intrinsic rewards proportional to τ t ​ ( s ) \tau_{t}(s) for under-visited states), model-learning budgets (allocating more environment interactions when SLEM detects bottleneck formation), or curriculum generation (reward-shift scheduling that targets the low-conductance regime where GTA-PS’s advantage is largest).

sections.heading: GPU acceleration and batching.
sections.text: Dense vector updates, sparse matrix-vector products, and Arnoldi iterations admit batching and GPU execution.

sections.heading: Unified design for the topology policy.
sections.text: The Boltzmann policy with fixed temperature b b is a pragmatic baseline that ensures ergodicity. Alternative topology-policy designs – such as learned attention policies that minimise SLEM, or topology policies designed to align with specific competitive baselines – could replace the softmax heuristic. The only invariant requirement is that the induced chain remains communicating with infinite-visit exploration.

sections.heading: D.1 Environment setup
sections.text: We use two environments that provide direct control over the relevant MDP characteristics. FourRooms [ 16 ] The tabular class FourRoomsTabular represents four rooms separated by walls and linked through one-cell corridors. Its default action set has size | 𝒜 | = 4 |\mathcal{A}|=4 , and the state space ranges from 20 20 to 120 120 passable cells. Most checked-in configurations use k ∈ { 1 , 4 } k\in\{1,4\} active rooms; a separate k = 2 k=2 setting supports fine-grained time-series measurements. The drift and one_way_prob arguments control transport asymmetry. GARNET [ 4 ] . The synthetic benchmark is the tabular class GarnetEnv . The checked-in configs use ( | 𝒮 | , | 𝒜 | ) = ( 75 , 4 ) (|\mathcal{S}|,|\mathcal{A}|)=(75,4) and ( 200 , 5 ) (200,5) , with branching factor 3 3 , neighbor-rate n_nbr_rate controlling locality, and optional dedicated reversible , bipartite , and reward_locality switches. Several experiment scripts also instantiate ad hoc GARNET settings with | 𝒮 | ∈ { 75,200 } |\mathcal{S}|\in\{75,200\} . This is the main environment for controlled sweeps over mixing rate, reversibility, reward support, and solver overhead. We construct various custom attributes on top of these base environments, such as mixing rate, reward span, reversibility factor, branching factor, and planning-budget effects under controlled nonstationarity.

sections.heading: D.2 Experiment Configurations
sections.text: All reported curves are aggregated over independent random seeds. The main orchestrator script suggest running the experiment on at least 1000 1000 seeds and ≥ 10 \geq 10 logical processors. Confidence bands are computed as 95 % 95\% Student- t t intervals over the seed means. Hyperparameter tuning uses the standalone Optuna driver [ 2 ] . Our tuning trial uses 200 200 trials with seed_offset =100000 so that tuning seeds stay disjoint from the evaluation seeds, therefore avoid inducing selection bias. For the deployed GTA-PS module, the numerical linear-solver tolerance is fixed across experiments: exact sparse LU is used for | 𝒮 | ≤ 300 |\mathcal{S}|\leq 300 , and otherwise the code switches to GMRES with restart = 30 =30 , maxiter = 500 =500 , and absolute tolerance atol = 10 − 4 10^{-4} , falling back to spsolve if GMRES returns nonzero status. For the Dyna host agent, an exploration rate ϵ = 0.2 \epsilon=0.2 is maintained to escape stale local loops, where the agent sample the current greedy action with probability 1 − ϵ 1-\epsilon and samples a random admissible action with probability ϵ \epsilon .

sections.heading: D.3 Reward protocol
sections.text: All environments use state-based rewards, but the reward pattern are designed to differ across setting purposes. FourRooms. The environment samples a Gaussian-mixture reward field instead of a single-cell goal. It chooses k k active rooms and places several Gaussian bumps in each selected room. The parameter n_peaks_per_room sets the number of bumps, and room_peak_ranges sets their room-specific heights. The final reward vector is normalized to unit maximum. Each reward shift resamples the field. GARNET. The default reward generator is sparse over reward_support states with amplitudes drawn uniformly from [ 0.5 , 1.5 ] [0.5,1.5] . When reward_locality=True , those rewarded states are drawn as a BFS-local connected cluster from the union graph of the transition tensor rather than as independent global samples.

sections.heading: D.4 Hyperparameters Tuning and Selection
sections.text: The repository includes a standalone Optuna tuner [ 2 ] . The selected configuration minimizes the mean L ∞ L_{\infty} value error to the exact DP solution over 30 30 tuning seeds, 4 4 reward shifts, K = 20 K=20 planning backups, and 50 50 host steps per shift. The exact hyperparameter search interval and tuned values are in the supplement code.

sections.heading: D.5 Baselines and fair-comparison controls
sections.text: The checked-in experiment harness instantiates three method variants: • standard_ps : the Moore-style prioritized-sweeping baseline [ 42 ] , using Bellman residual magnitude as the queue key. • gta_base : GTA-PS with fixed α \alpha and fixed β \beta . • gta_beta : GTA-PS with fixed α \alpha and adaptive β t \beta_{t} . All three variants are implemented through the unified priority-based planning interface B.3 The unified Prioritized Sweeping interface . This lets us run them under the exact same host setting, MDP instance, backup budget, and evaluation protocol, with no method-specific entanglement. The differences can only happen in their inner states themselves.

sections.heading: D.6 Why no baselines apart from Standard-PS?
sections.text: We use Standard-PS as the sole direct baseline because it is the only comparison that matches our assumption set and intervention scope without introducing additional confounds. Similar works discussed in the paper, including TVI [ 21 ] , VaST [ 20 ] , Dyna-2 [ 56 ] , or Generalized Prioritized Solver (GPS) [ 68 ] are therefore are not really click as direct baselines. Under the communicating-MDP assumption, TVI effectively reduces to a Standard-PS update schedule. VaST introduces supervised representation learning, which is orthogonal to our fixed-MDP priority-design setting. Dyna-2 and concerns host-agent architecture and model-based decision organization, whereas our study focuses only on the management of sequential value backups inside a given planning interface. Generalized prioritized solvers [ 68 ] is the most close candidate, with a priority score of Value-plus-error. However, the issue of stale value-function entries (by nonstationary rewards) misleading the queue is clear logically. In one hand, we have empirically observed that value-function can barely adapts in a reasonable pace E.2 Additional ablations . In the other hand, GPS was shown to degrade under environments with a high dose of stochasticity, in which our method holds close performance from standard PS 6 . We instead use these methods as major contextual guidances, which aids our grasp in the setting of nonstationary RL.

sections.heading: Sparse representation.
sections.text: The topology module stores the policy-induced systems in SciPy sparse form. In GtaPS , P π P_{\pi} is converted to CSR, near-zero entries below 10 − 12 10^{-12} are dropped, and the forward system is assembled as ( 1 + η ) ​ I − P π (1+\eta)I-P_{\pi} . The in-field system uses in_laplacian(P_pi) with an additional diagonal stabilizer of η + 10 − 6 \eta+10^{-6} in the initialization and lazy-rebuild path.

sections.heading: Solver selection in the deployed module.
sections.text: The experiment implementation uses the threshold _LU_THRESHOLD = 300 . For | 𝒮 | ≤ 300 |\mathcal{S}|\leq 300 , both forward and backward systems are factored with scipy.sparse.linalg.splu and then reused for all subsequent solves. For | 𝒮 | > 300 |\mathcal{S}|>300 , the module calls gmres with restart=30 , maxiter=500 , and atol=1e-8 , with a fallback to spsolve if GMRES reports nonzero status. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.06186v1 [cs.LG] 05 Sep 2026 Spectral Prioritized Sweeping in Non-stationary Reinforcement Learning Hung Pham Affiliation: SOICT, Hanoi University of Science and Technology Email: hungpg230036@sis.hust.edu.vn Tuan Dam Affiliation: SOICT, Hanoi University of Science and Technology Email: tuandq@soict.hust.edu.vn Abstract Prioritized Sweeping (PS) accelerates model-based reinforcement learning by selecting backups according to Bellman residual magnitude. In nonstationary reward settings, however, the canonical priority score is shortsighted: after a localized reward shift, residuals propagate only through realized backups, so bottlenecked or topologically distant state estimates may remain static under a limited replanning budget. We introduce the Graph Topology Augmentation framework, which employ the graph’s resolvent and its diffusion semantic, to augment the inquired signal. Our application, Graph Topology Augmentation for Prioritized Sweeping (GTA-PS), or which the alias Spectral Prioritized Sweeping (SPS) might be more universal, provides a drop-in ordering score for the setting of fixed dynamics and changing state rewards. GTA-PS uses a smootherized policy, inducing a transition chain, with its in- and out-Laplacian. The standard priority key is augmented with a mixing of regularized Laplacian inverses diffusing the residual magnitude. Furthermore, the topology contribution is annealed by a scheduler based on the Second Largest Eigenvalue Modulus (SLEM), allowing its scale to adapt to the chain’s mixing regime. We prove that the forward potential coincides with geometric discounted residual propagation and show that GTA-PS gives active priority instantly to all states. Tabular experiments on FourRooms and GARNET domains demonstrate improved replanning efficiency over standard PS under both exact DP and Dyna-style host planners. 1 Introduction Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) improves general behavior by using a known or learned transition model for planning [ 59 , Ch. 8] . The agent benefits most when planning effort can be directed to the states that matter most, especially within a brittle planning budget. [ 61 , 30 ] . Prioritized Sweeping (PS, or Standard-PS as to distinguish from our introduced variants) addresses this by maintaining a queue of states keyed by Bellman or Temporal-Difference residual magnitude [ 42 , 45 ] . For each planning step, the state with the largest priority has its value estimate updated. After that, predecessors’ value estimates often increase in magnitude; their refreshed priorities have higher chance to be queried next. This effect encourages information propagation backward through the predecessor support graph. Although conceptually simple, the resulting sweep can improve update efficiency by several orders of magnitude compared to uniform random backups [ 68 ] . We focus our study in the case of nonstationary Markov Decision Process (MDP), where the transition dynamics are fixed but the state reward changes over time [ 44 ] . This setting appears whenever the navigation structure is comparatively stable but the task objective changes, as in goal-conditioned robotics [ 46 ] , dynamic pricing and operations settings [ 5 ] , and sequential recommendation problems [ 70 ] . The standard approach using residual priority is shortsighted and reactive , as most state order remain stale until the Bellman wave has propagated to them through concrete realized backups. Under the budget of K K updates between reward shifts, some topologically distant states may never be reached, regardless of how sophisticated the host planner is [ 59 ] . In the nonstationary setting of our focus, this creates a further hindsight effect: by the time the residual signal reaches distant regions, the reward information that triggered it may already be stale. The resulting value errors can then feed back into the planning–action loop, causing the host to allocate future updates according to outdated priorities, compound into a circular degradation of both planning quality and subsequent data collection [ 15 , 33 ] . Figure 1: A localized reward shift creates sparse residual at s r s_{r} . Standard PS is shortsighted: priority of distant states receives no information hints. GTA-PS adds a topology potential on the policy-induced graph, assigning priority to upstream states before predecessor pushes reach them. We propose to address the former hindrance – credit propagation – by utilizing the model as assignment guidance. The Graph Topology Augmentation (GTA) framework capture preferences of the agent’s navigation field using spectral operators. From that, we derive rich representations and signal preconditioning that can be used to augment available score-based decisions, such as credit assignment, or bandit identification. Graph Topology Augmentation for Prioritized Sweeping (GTA-PS) is an implementation of the GTA ideology for our nonstationary setting study, that augment the residual-keyed priority with an additive mixed terms constructed from directed Laplacian inverses. The method is broadly applicable to orthogonal techniques, such as functional approximation, partial observability, and model uncertainty. Our contributions. • We formalize priority-based planning as a host-agnostic queue-management problem, making the priority definition a modular design choice. The revised planning module plugs seamlessly into both exact tabular (DP) and Dyna-style planners without modifying the host. • We introduce Graph Topology Augmentation (GTA), a general RL framework that applies spectral operators on policy-induced chains to produce topology-aware planning signals. • We present GTA-PS (with the alias SPS), a concrete GTA instantiation for nonstationary rewards. It augments residual priority with a directed regularized-Laplacian potential and a fixed forward/backward weight aggregation together with a SLEM-driven β t \beta_{t} scheduler that adapts topology gain to the chain’s mixing regime. • We prove key properties of the topology signal, including its numerical stability, the geometric discount and implicit importance sampling effects, plus SLEM adaptive capabilities. • We present a succint experimental evaluation, variating chain statistics across environments and planner architectures, with surgical ablations isolating each cause’s effectiveness. 2 Related Work In model-based planning, three lines of work have been established to provide richer planning guidance beyond raw residual magnitude, aiding prioritized sweeping decision. Successor-based signals spread value information over the state graph rather than waiting for purely local error cascades [ 22 , 58 ] . Learned abstractions compress the planning space, utilizing the generalization capabilities of supervised learning, as in VaST ’s abstract tabular model [ 20 ] . Graph-structural heuristics uses auxiliary graph representation, as in TVI/FTVI , which exploit the strongly connected components decomposition of the MDP [ 21 ] . Together these demonstrate that good planning requires more than raw residuals and that model knowledge is a powerful source of leadership. Spectral graph theory has a long history of applications in RL representation learning. Proto-value functions [ 39 , 38 ] use undirected Laplacian eigenvectors as smooth value-approximation bases [ 55 , 7 ] . The same eigenvectors underpin option discovery [ 36 ] and its deep analogues via the successor representation [ 37 ] and cover-time options [ 32 ] . Scalable computational methods include Krylov-subspace methods such as Arnoldi and GMRES [ 27 , 48 ] , Graph-drawing objectives with unique solutions [ 66 ] , and recent exact recovery methods [ 28 ] . Recent concurrent work on effective resistance has proposed it as an intrinsic reward guiding agents toward structurally accessible goals [ 14 ] . In these works, spectral operators mainly serve as offline representation or filtering bases rather than as a direct mechanism for shaping online backup selection. Our proposed Graph Topology Augmentation framework brings analytical Markov-chain tools into an RL planning module. It builds on the Laplacian-potential intuition from electrical networks [ 24 ] , treating the policy-induced chain as the Laplacian kernel [ 19 ] and its Green’s function as the potential operator [ 18 ] . Eigenvalues of the directed chain [ 35 ] is utilized as a scheduling signal. Additionally, several analytical tools such as biorthogonal decomposition [ 29 ] , additive reversibility decomposition [ 12 ] , and classical spectral graph bounds [ 17 ] are investigated to further enrich the framework. 3 Preliminary Markov Decision Processes.
